en: Compiled by the National Preceptor of the Chen and Sui Dynasties, the Great Master Zhizhe.
21. The First Gate of the Nine Contemplations of Loathsomeness (Navasubhāsmṛti), Part Twenty-One.
1. The Contemplation of Swelling; 2. The Contemplation of the Livid-Blue; 3. The Contemplation of Putrefaction; 4. The Contemplation of Blood.

1. The perception of a smeared corpse; 2. the perception of a bloated corpse; 3. the perception of a festering corpse; 4. the perception of a discolored corpse; 5. the perception of a worm-infested corpse; 6. the perception of a mangled corpse; 7. the perception of a scattered corpse; 8. the perception of a skeleton; 9. the perception of a burned corpse.
These are followed by the dhyāna of universal clarity (*sāmānyaprabhāsa*). Thus are the nine perceptions explained.
The dhyāna explained above,
although possessing concentration and wisdom,
is merely a contemplation of reality.
As long as one has not yet attained the contemplation that brings liberation,
the power of the antidote remains weak;
this is the case from the nine perceptions onward.
The meditative concentrations explained herein all possess contemplations that lead to liberation;
they serve as remedies for the disease of heavy afflictions.
The power of application is what constitutes strength.
It is like felling a hard tree:
if one uses a soft axe, [it will not succeed].
If one cannot sever it,
one should take up a stronger axe;
for the nine perceptions (*navasaṃjñā*) are the initial stage of attaining liberation through contemplation.
Therefore, we shall next analyze this: these nine are collectively termed "perception" (*saṃjñā*) because they are capable of transforming the mind and transforming perception;
thus, they are called "perception."
These are called the meditations that can overturn impure and inverted perceptions;
therefore, these nine dharmas are all termed "perceptions" (*saṃjñā*).
First, the perception of bloating: if one contemplates a human corpse...
The body swells like a leather bag filled with wind,
its appearance altered from its original state;
this is the perception of bloating.
2. The Perception of the Livid (vinīlaka-saṃjñā):
If one contemplates a corpse whose skin and flesh have become yellowish-red, livid, black, or dark blue, this is the perception of the livid.
Third, the perception of disintegration:
if one contemplates a corpse that has been blown by the wind and scorched by the sun until it becomes increasingly torn and disintegrated, lying upon the ground.
This is the perception of the disintegrated.
Fourth is the perception of being smeared with blood: when one contemplates a corpse, pus and blood are seen overflowing everywhere.
It is smeared and defiled;
this is the perception of being smeared with blood.
Fifth, the perception of putrefaction: if one contemplates a corpse...
Worms and pus flow out;
the skin and flesh are rotted away,
streaming profusely upon the ground.
This is the perception of festering pus.
Sixth, the perception of being devoured: if one contemplates a corpse being gnawed and eaten by maggots.
Birds peck out their eyes;
foxes and dogs chew them;
tigers and wolves tear them apart—this is the perception of devouring (khādyaka-saṃjñā).
Seventh, the contemplation of disintegration: if one contemplates a corpse that has been torn apart by birds and beasts,
its physical form shattered and scattered.
The tendons are severed, the bones are disarticulated, and the head and hands lie scattered across one another; this is the contemplation of dispersion.
Eighth is the contemplation of bones: if one contemplates a corpse...
The skin and flesh have completely vanished;
only white bones remain,
their tendons either still connected or scattered in disarray.
Like a conch shell or like a white jade disk—this is the perception of bones.
Ninth, the perception of burning: if one contemplates a corpse being consumed by fire.
The stench of bursting smoke spreads;
when the fuel is exhausted, the form is extinguished,
becoming one with the ashes and dust.
Even if they are not burned,
they likewise return to extinction;
this is the perception of burning.

22. The First Gate of the Eight Recollections (Aṣṭānu-smṛti), the Twenty-second. 1. Recollection of the Buddha; 2. Recollection of the Dharma; 3. Recollection of the Saṃgha; 4. Recollection of the Precepts; 5. Recollection of Renunciation; 6. Recollection of the Devas; 7. Recollection of Inhalation and Exhalation; 8. Recollection of Death. Regarding the explanation of the eight recollections following the nine perceptions (*navasaṃjñā*): [the text continues as follows:]... [The passage concludes with the enumeration of the eight recollections.]
This is for the purpose of eliminating fear.
When practicing the nine contemplations on loathsomeness,
one reflects upon the corpse as something repulsive.
Therefore, they were struck with terror;
their hair stood on end in agitation,
and they were further tormented by evil Māras.
Their anxiety and fear will increase further;
however, if they maintain their minds upon the eight recollections,
their terror will immediately be dispelled.
Therefore, it is placed next [to mindfulness]. Generally speaking,
"recollection" (smṛti) is another name for the internal mind's act of retaining and remembering.
Because one focuses the mind to recollect these eight kinds of merit,
they are called the "Eight Recollections.
They are not only able to eliminate worldly fears and terrors.
If one can cultivate this skillfully, it will also eliminate all obstacles and difficulties of birth and death within the three realms of the world.
First, the Recitation of the Buddha: when encountering terror or various obstacles and difficulties, [one should recite].
One should practice mindfulness of the Buddha.
The Buddha is the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha;
his divine virtues are immeasurable.
Having reflected thus, fears, obstacles, and difficulties are immediately eliminated.
Second, mindfulness of the Dharma: when there are times of fear, obstacles, or difficulties.
One should be mindful of the Dharma.
The Buddha-Dharma skillfully brings forth results in this very life, free from feverish affliction;
it does not depend on time and can lead one to a wholesome destination.
To attain unimpeded penetration is the recollection of the Dharma.
Third is the recollection of the Sangha. Regarding the recollection of the Sangha:
The Sangha is the community of the Buddha’s disciples.
They are fully endowed with the fivefold Dharma-body (pañca-dharmakāya),
within which there are four pairs and eight ranks.
Those who have attained the fruits of the three vehicles should receive offerings and veneration;
they are the unsurpassed fields of merit in the world.
This is the increase of mindfulness.
Fourth is mindfulness of precepts. As for mindfulness of precepts:
precepts are that which can obstruct all evils.
It is a dwelling place of peace and security.
Within this, there are three kinds of precepts:
namely, the precept of restraint (*saṃvara-śīla*), the precept concurrent with meditative concentration (*dhyāna-sahaja-śīla*), and the precept concurrent with the Path (*mārga-sahaja-śīla*).
The restraint of ethical discipline (*śīla-saṃvara*) can eliminate all evils of body and speech;
that which is conjoined with meditative concentration (*samādhi-sahagata*) can obstruct the evil thoughts of afflictions (*kleśa*);
and that which is conjoined with the Path (*mārga-sahagata*) can destroy ignorance (*avidyā*).
One attains liberation through wisdom.
This is mindfulness of precepts.
Regarding the five recollections on relinquishment: as for mindfulness of relinquishment—
There are two kinds:
first, the relinquishment of giving;
second, the relinquishment of afflictions.
The relinquishment of giving gives rise to great merit;
the relinquishment of afflictions [gives rise to liberation].
Thus one attains wisdom and enters nirvana;
this is the mindfulness of relinquishment (*tyāgānusmṛti*).
The six recollections of the devas: as for the recollection of the devas (*devānusmṛti*):
That is to say, from the Heaven of the Four Great Kings up to the Heaven of Mastery over Others' Emanations;
furthermore, there are four kinds of heavens.
First is the Heaven of Heaven, second is the Heaven Born of Heaven, third is the Pure Heaven, and fourth is the Heaven Born of Purity.
Such are the purities of karmic fruition,
which bring benefit and peace to all.
This is mindfulness of the devas.
Seventh is mindfulness of ānāpāna. As for mindfulness of ānāpāna, it is as explained in the sixteen stages of special excellence (ṣoḍaśa-viśeṣa).
When one maintains mindfulness in this way regarding the inhalation and exhalation of breath,
one is able to eliminate mental distraction and enter the right path.
How much more so regarding worldly terrors;
this is the mindfulness of *ānāpānasmṛti* (mindfulness of breathing).
Eighth is the mindfulness of death: as for the mindfulness of death—
There are two kinds of death:
first, death by one's own accord;
second, death due to external causes.
These two kinds of death constantly follow this body;
there is no place where one may avoid them.

This is the recollection of death. 23. The First Gate of the Ten Perceptions (Daśasaṃjñā): Second Part of the First Gate. 1. Perception of Impermanence; 2. Perception of Suffering; 3. Perception of Non-self; 4. Perception of the Impurity of Food; 5. Perception of the Unattractiveness of the World; 6. Perception of Death; 7. Perception of Impurity; 8. Perception of Cessation; 9. Perception of Detachment; 10. Perception of Exhaustion. Regarding the exposition of the ten perceptions following the eight recollections:
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"The nine perceptions are like binding a thief; the ten perceptions are like killing a thief.
If this is so, they should have been explained immediately following the preceding nine perceptions.
However, because there are obstacles such as fear when practicing the nine notions (navasaṃjñā),
it is necessary to teach the eight recollections (aṣṭasmṛti).
Having attained freedom from all fears,
the mind becomes peaceful and unobstructed;
therefore, the ten perceptions are explained next.
Generally speaking, "perception" (saṃjñā) refers to that which can transform the mind and transform perception;
it is capable of transforming the conceptualization of permanence, bliss, and so forth.
Because it consists of various inverted perceptions and so forth,
it is called "perception" (saṃjñā).
The first three types of perception are taught for the purpose of severing the afflictions pertaining to the truths (satyadarśana-heya-kleśa).
The middle four perceptions are taught for the purpose of severing the afflictions through contemplation;
the latter three perceptions are taught for those practicing the path of no-more-learning. Therefore:
A person who destroys [defiled] dharmas and cultivates these ten perceptions can sever the fetters and latent tendencies of the three realms.
This is the realization of the noble fruit of outflowlessness (*anāsrava*).
First, the perception of impermanence (*anitya-saṃjñā*): it is the perception associated with wisdom that contemplates all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) as impermanent.
This is called the perception of impermanence.
All conditioned phenomena are of two kinds:
first, sentient beings.
Second is the realm.
Both of these arise and perish in every moment;
therefore, they are impermanent.
Second, the perception of suffering: the perception associated with wisdom that contemplates all conditioned phenomena as suffering is called the perception of suffering.
If conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) are impermanent,
they are suffering because they are constantly oppressed and driven by the three types of suffering and the eight types of suffering; therefore,
they are called "suffering."
The perception of non-self in the three [realms]: contemplating all phenomena as equally being without self;
this perception associated with wisdom is called the perception of non-self.
If all conditioned phenomena are suffering,
they are without self because they lack sovereignty;
furthermore, since suffering arises from conditions, it lacks intrinsic nature.
Within the absence of intrinsic nature, a self cannot be found.
Regarding the perception of impurity in the four kinds of nutriment: contemplate all food and drink as impure.
The perception associated with wisdom is called the perception of the impurity of food;
this refers to worldly food and drink.
All arise from impure causes and conditions;
thus, there are things such as flesh produced from semen and blood, or ghee and curd produced from water and milk.
All these should likewise be contemplated according to their specific nature.
All these are impure.
Fifth is the perception of the world as unattractive: one contemplates all worlds as unattractive, a perception associated with wisdom.
This is called the perception of the world as unattractive.
There are two kinds of worlds:
first, the world of sentient beings.
Second is the land, which has faults and evils and is not a place for enjoyment.
(6) The perception of death: the perception associated with the wisdom that contemplates death.
This is called the perception of death.
If one’s karmic retribution for a single lifetime is constantly pursued by these two kinds of death, [one should cultivate this perception].
Thus, one does not exhale until the inhalation has been completed.
The seven perceptions of impurity: contemplating the impurity of one's own body and the bodies of others;
these are perceptions associated with wisdom.
This is called the perception of impurity.
If one contemplates that within this body there are thirty-six substances,
and externally there are nine orifices.
Impure blood constantly flows;
from birth until death,
there is not a single moment of purity.
The eight perceptions of abandonment: contemplating nirvana as being free from birth and death,
this perception associated with wisdom is called the perception of abandonment.
The practitioner reflects:
"If nirvana is pure and free from afflictions,"
One should sever the fetters and realize nirvana.
Ninth, the perception of detachment: contemplating that nirvana is detached from birth-and-death;
this is the perception associated with wisdom.
This is called the "conception of detachment.
The practitioner contemplates:
"If nirvana is pure..."
"One who departs from birth and death" means that one should depart from birth and death to realize nirvāṇa.
The ten perceptions of exhaustion (*daśa-kṣaya-saṃjñā*): one contemplates the exhaustion of the fetters (*saṃyojana*), as well as the exhaustion of birth and death, within nirvāṇa.
The perception associated with wisdom is called the perception of exhaustion.
The practitioner contemplates it thus.
If nirvāṇa were pure,
then as for the fetters and saṃsāra— so long as those fetters have not been exhausted— [it would not be pure].
And [it concerns] the karma of birth and death, and the realization of nirvāṇa.

24. The First Gate of the Eight Liberations (Aṣṭavimokṣa), Part Two. 1. Having the perception of internal forms, one perceives external forms; 2. Having no perception of internal forms, one perceives external forms; 3. The liberation of the beautiful, personally realized by the body; 4. The liberation of the sphere of infinite space; 5. The liberation of the sphere of infinite consciousness; 6. The liberation of the sphere of nothingness; 7. The liberation of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; 8. The liberation of the cessation of sensation and perception. Regarding the explanation of the eight liberations following the ten perceptions (*daśasaṃjñā*):...
The preceding nine and ten contemplations (saṃjñās),
being meditative gateways that serve as antidotes to the phenomena of disintegration,
are thus restricted horizontally and short in their vertical progression.
The meditative concentrations that serve as antidotes for observing the various dhyānas are all incomplete;
however, if one realizes the fruit of sainthood, they become fully perfected.
Consequently, there would be no great virtues such as the three types of clear knowledge (trividyā) and the eight liberations (aṣṭavimokṣa).
Now, I wish to fully elucidate all the untainted (anāsrava) antidotes.
Because one contemplates, trains, perfumes,
and cultivates meditative concentration, it is explained next;
if one practices this contemplation.
Having cultivated the various dhyānas and samādhis,
at the time of realizing the fruit of sainthood,
one becomes a powerful arhat endowed with the six superknowledges (ṣaḍabhijñā) and the three insights (trividyā).
As well as the eight liberations,
the knowledge of vows, the peak dhyānas,
the samādhi of non-contention, and so forth.
These are all meritorious qualities.
Regarding why these eight are collectively termed "liberations" (*prātimokṣa*),
the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
To turn one's back on these pure five sensual desires and abandon this mind of attachment is therefore called "turning away" (*prātikūlya-vairāgya*).
If one gives rise to true,
untainted wisdom and exhausts the fetters and karma of the three realms,
this is precisely what is called liberation.

First, having the perception of internal forms while externally perceiving forms: "having the perception of internal forms" means not destroying internal form and not extinguishing the perception of internal form.
Regarding external forms: one does not destroy external forms,
nor does one extinguish the characteristics of external forms.
One contemplates external forms with this impure mind;
the reason for doing so is to cultivate the radiance of light.
One should not, within the first liberation (*vimokṣa*), destroy the internal body or the skeleton-man.
Because the fetters and latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of the desire realm are difficult to sever,
one must employ a mind of impurity to contemplate external forms.
This first liberation (vimokṣa) is situated in the first dhyāna;
because it is able to relinquish both oneself and others, as well as the lower stages,
it is called "liberation."

Second, having no perception of internal forms, one perceives external forms. "Having no perception of internal forms" means that one has eliminated internal form and extinguished the perception of internal form.
Regarding external forms: one does not destroy external forms,
nor does one extinguish the characteristics of external forms.
One contemplates external forms with this mind of impurity.
The reason for doing so is that the practitioner seeks to enter the internal purity of the second dhyāna.
One contemplates the internal skeleton in order to destroy it,
for the fetters and latent tendencies of the desire realm are difficult to sever;
thus, one still observes the signs of external impurity.
The third is the pure liberation, which one realizes through the body. It is called "pure" because its object is pure.
As for the practitioner:
having set aside the signs of impurity, [they contemplate purity].
However, within meditative concentration,
one refines the eightfold radiant light until it is pure and brilliant, like the color of a wondrous jewel.
Therefore, it is called "realizing the purity of the body through conditions.
Because one experiences the pervasive bodily bliss within the third dhyāna with a mind free from attachment and grasping, it is called "realizing it with the body."
The liberation of the sphere of infinite space: if one eliminates the form of the fundamental fourth dhyāna,
as well as the forms within the three liberations, the four bases of mastery,
and the eight spheres of totality.
With single-minded focus, one enters meditative concentration by taking infinite space as the object;
one then contemplates that this concentration, being dependent upon the aggregates, sense bases, and elements, is impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self, and is deceptive and unreal.
The mind gives rise to revulsion and turns away from them,
refusing to accept or cling to them;
it enters deeply into a single direction without turning back.
This is the liberation of the sphere of infinite space.

Regarding the liberation of the sphere of infinite consciousness: when one relinquishes the sphere of infinite space and enters meditative absorption with the mind focused single-mindedly on consciousness, it is [the liberation of the sphere of infinite consciousness].
One then contemplates this meditative concentration:
because it depends upon the aggregates (skandhas), bases (āyatanas),
and elements (dhātus), it is impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self.
Being false and unreal,
one gives rise to a mind of aversion and does not accept or cling to them.
Entering deeply and single-mindedly without turning back—this is the liberation of the sphere of infinite consciousness.
Regarding the liberation of the sphere of nothingness: if one relinquishes consciousness.
When entering meditative concentration by focusing the mind on non-existence,
one then contemplates this concentration in terms of the aggregates,
sense bases, and elements.
Therefore, there is impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self;
they are deceptive and unreal,
giving rise to a mind of weary revulsion.
Without experiencing attachment,
one enters deeply and single-mindedly without turning back;
this is the liberation through the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana-vimokṣa*).
The seventh liberation, which is neither-perception-nor-non-perception:
when one relinquishes the sphere of nothingness and, with a single mind, takes the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception as an object and enters meditative absorption.
One then contemplates this meditative concentration:
because it relies upon the aggregates, sense bases, and elements,
it is characterized by impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self.
Being false and unreal,
one gives rise to a mind of revulsion and turns away from them,
rather than accepting or clinging to them.
Entering deeply and single-mindedly without turning back—this is the liberation of "neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Eighth is the liberation of the cessation of feeling and perception: it is the turning away from and the cessation of feeling, perception, and all mental states and mental factors.
This is the liberation through the cessation of sensation and perception;
why is this so? Because the disciples of the Buddhas are weary of and loathe a distracted mind.
Desiring to enter meditative absorption for rest,
he established the dharma of nirvāṇa within his body.
Therefore it is said: "The body is realized, and perception and feeling are extinguished. 25.

The First Gate of the Eight Bases of Mastery (Aṣṭa-abhibhvāyatana). The First Gate of the Eight Bases of Mastery, Number Twenty-Five: Internally perceiving forms, one externally perceives forms that are few.
Whether beautiful or ugly—
this is called superior knowledge and superior vision. Second, having the perception of internal forms, one perceives external forms as manifold,
whether beautiful or ugly.

These are called superior knowledge and superior vision: (3) internally perceiving no form, one perceives forms externally that are few; likewise, (4) internally perceiving no form, one perceives forms externally that are many; (5) the blue sphere of mastery; (6) the yellow sphere of mastery; (7) the red sphere of mastery; and (8) the white sphere of mastery—these follow the eight liberations (*aṣṭavimokṣa*).
Regarding the explanation of the eight bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*):
although the liberations (*vimokṣa*) possess the function of turning away from and abandoning the five objects of desire,
they are nonetheless the initial stages of contemplation.
While transforming within objective conditions,
one has not yet attained mastery over the mind according to one's will.
If one wishes to attain proficiency in the contemplation of the mind, [one must practice].
To attain mastery over transformation,
one must necessarily advance in the cultivation of the contemplation of the superior bases (*abhibhvāyatana*).
Therefore, these are explained next.
Therefore, the Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra provides an analogy, saying:
"It is like a person riding a horse who can both break through the enemy lines and also control that horse himself."
Therefore, they are called the "Stages of Mastery" (abhibhvāyatana).
They are also called the "Eight Bases of Removal" (aṣṭau kṛtsnāyatanāni).
The first is: internally perceiving forms, one externally perceives forms that are limited.
Whether beautiful or ugly,
this is called superior knowledge and superior vision: having the perception of internal forms,
one perceives external forms as limited.
Regarding the "lesser" (parītta) in the context of the first liberation:
it is called "lesser" because its object is limited;
this applies when the path of observation has not yet increased.
Therefore, one must contemplate limited causes and conditions; when contemplating the vastness of fear and difficulty, the transformations cannot be controlled at will.
However, if one contemplates the impurity within limited phenomena—whether beautiful or ugly—one gains mastery over these transformations.
He penetrates all things without obstruction;
his mind is free from grasping;
he does not give rise to craving when renouncing.
This aversion is called superior knowledge and superior vision.
Second, having the perception of internal forms, one perceives external forms as many,
whether beautiful or ugly.
This is called superior knowledge and superior vision: internally perceiving the mark of form while externally perceiving forms.
Regarding the statement "many" in the first liberation, it refers to observing many causes and conditions.
Therefore, it is called "much contemplation.
Once the mind is thus disciplined,
there is no hindrance to much contemplation.
Therefore, it is said that there is much [transformation].
If one possesses mastery over transforming many objects— whether beautiful, ugly, or impure—
[this is called the power of transformation].
They attain unimpeded penetration;
their minds are free from grasping or rejecting,
and they give rise neither to attachment nor to aversion.
This is called superior knowledge and superior vision.
Third, being internally without the perception of form, one perceives forms externally that are limited,
whether beautiful or ugly.
This is called superior knowledge and superior vision: internally perceiving no signs of form, like the two liberations (vimokṣas),
one externally perceives forms that are few,
whether beautiful or ugly, and so forth.
In all these cases, it is as in the first stage of mastery.
Fourth, being internally without the perception of form, one perceives external forms,
whether beautiful or ugly.
This is called superior knowledge and superior vision: internally perceiving no signs of form, as in the two liberations,
one externally perceives forms that are manifold,
whether beautiful or ugly, and so forth.
These are all like the two superior bases (abhibhvāyatana).
Regarding the fifth superior base, the blue: if one contemplates the color blue, one attains mastery over its transformation.
What is small can become large, and what is large can become small.
Its radiant luster surpasses that of the liberations (*vimokṣa*).
Furthermore, one does not give rise to craving for dharmas regarding the perceived sign of blue.
This is called the superior sphere of blue.
The six superior spheres of yellow are to be distinguished in the same manner as those in the section on the superior sphere of blue.
The seven superior spheres of red are to be distinguished in the same manner as those in the section on the superior sphere of blue.
The eight white spheres of mastery (*śubha-krtsnāyatana*) are also to be distinguished in the same manner as the blue spheres of mastery.
Here, four colors are employed as the spheres of mastery,
according to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.
In the *Sragdharā-sūtra*, however, the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) are taken as the four spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*).

**Chapter 26: The First Gate of the Ten Spheres of Totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*)** 1. The sphere of total blue (*nīla-kṛtsnāyatana*) 2. The sphere of total yellow (*pīta-kṛtsnāyatana*) 3. The sphere of total red (*lohita-kṛtsnāyatana*) 4. The sphere of total white (*avadāta-kṛtsnāyatana*) 5. The sphere of total earth (*pṛthivī-kṛtsnāyatana*) 6. The sphere of total water (*ap-kṛtsnāyatana*) 7. The sphere of total fire (*tejas-kṛtsnāyatana*) 8. The sphere of total wind (*vāyu-kṛtsnāyatana*) 9. The sphere of total space (*ākāśa-kṛtsnāyatana*) 10. The sphere of total consciousness (*vijñāna-kṛtsnāyatana*) Regarding the explanation of the ten spheres of totality following the eight spheres of mastery: [text continues]
Although the spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) enable one to exercise mastery over transformations within meditative observation to a small degree, they are not yet universal;
now, in the ten spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*), that which is observed is universal.
Therefore, I shall clarify this in sequence.
Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"The liberations (*vimokṣa*) constitute the initial gateway."
The spheres of mastery (abhibhvāyatana) constitute the middle stage of practice;
the spheres of totality (kṛtsnāyatana) constitute its accomplishment.
These are the three types of sufficient conditions for contemplation (manasikāra-paryāpti).
This refers to the accomplishment of the essence of meditative observation (*vipaśyanā*).
As for the general designation "pervading all places," it is named after the pervasive nature of the object of observation.
These are also called the ten *kṛtsnāyatanas* (totalities).

First is the blue totality: one takes the slight blue color from among the previously mentioned *abhibhvāyatanas* (mastery bases) and *vimokṣas* (liberations), causing it to pervade all places so that everything becomes blue.

Second, the yellow universal base (*pīta-kṛtsnāyatana*): one again takes the slight yellow color from among the previously mentioned liberations (*vimokṣa*) and bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), causing it to pervade all places so that everything becomes yellow.
Third, the red universal base (*lohita-kṛtsnāyatana*): one again takes the slight red color from among the previously mentioned liberations and bases of mastery.
One causes all places to be entirely red. Fourth, the white universal base:
one again takes the small amount of white from among the previously mentioned liberations (*vimokṣa*) and spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), causing all places to be entirely white.

The fifth is the totality of earth (*pṛthivī-kṛtsnāyatana*): one again takes the limited earth-form from among the previously mentioned liberations (*vimokṣa*) and spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), causing the entire field to become earth-form.
The sixth is the totality of water (*ap-kṛtsnāyatana*): one again takes the limited water-form from among the previously mentioned liberations and spheres of mastery.
One causes all places to appear as the color of water.

Regarding the seven fire-totalities (*tejo-kasiṇa*): one again takes the slight color of fire from among the previously mentioned liberations (*vimokṣa*) and spheres of mastery (*abhibhv-āyatana*), causing all places to appear as the color of fire.

Regarding the eighth, the sphere of all wind: one again takes up the minor aspect of the color of wind from among the previous liberations and spheres of mastery, causing the entire sphere to consist of the color of wind.
Regarding the ninth, the sphere of all space: one re-enters the previously attained meditative concentration of the liberation of space.
One causes all places to be empty.
Regarding the "perception of all places": one returns to the sphere of the preceding perception and attains liberation.
One causes all places to possess perception.

27. The First Gate of the Fourteen Transformations (Caturdaśa-nirmāṇa-prathama-mukha), Chapter Twenty-seven. There are two transformations in the first dhyāna, three transformations in the second dhyāna, four transformations in the third dhyāna, and five transformations in the fourth dhyāna; these constitute the fourteen transformations. Following this, the fourteen transformations are explained by means of the ten spheres of totality (daśa-kṛtsnāyatana).
The contemplation of dhyāna explained above,
though complete in its essential nature, has not yet had its functional efficacy distinguished.
Now, one wishes to learn the application of the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*).
One must first cultivate the mind of transformation (*nirmāṇacitta*).
Generally speaking, "transformation" refers to the ability to cause that which is non-existent to suddenly appear, and that which exists to suddenly vanish.
Therefore, it is called "transformation" (nirmāṇa).
There are two types: first, the dhyāna; second, transformation. Regarding the first, the dhyāna, there is the transformation of the first dhyāna, which is able to transform within its own stage.

1. Those in the first dhyāna who possess the power of transformation from the desire realm can transform objects belonging to the lower stage of the desire realm. 2. Those in the second dhyāna have three types of transformations:
a. Those in the first dhyāna transform objects of the first dhyāna; b. Those in the second dhyāna transform objects of the second dhyāna.
One can transform things within one's own level.
Second, those in the second dhyāna can transform things in the first dhyāna;
they can transform things in the lower level of the first dhyāna.
The three [meditations] and the second dhyāna transform the desire realm;
they are able to manifest transformations in the lower stage of the desire realm.
The third dhyāna has four transformations: first, the third dhyāna manifests transformations within the third dhyāna.
One can transform within one's own stage.
In the second and third dhyānas, one transforms within the second dhyāna;
one can transform within the lower two dhyāna stages.
The first dhyāna of the three dhyānas transforms;
it can transform [beings] of the lower first-dhyāna level.
The fourth dhyāna of the three dhyānas transforms [beings] of the desire realm.
One can transform [beings] in the lower realms of the desire world.
Regarding the four dhyānas and the five types of transformation: first, the four dhyānas transform within the four dhyānas;
they can transform within their own respective stages.
The transformations of the second, fourth,
and third dhyānas can manifest the stages of the three lower dhyānas; the transformations of the third and fourth dhyānas can manifest the stage of the second dhyāna.
One can transform the lower two dhyāna stages.
The fourth [dhyāna] transforms the first dhyāna;
one can transform the lower first dhyāna stage.
The fifth and fourth [meditative absorptions] transform the desire realm; they are able to produce transformations in the lower stages of the desire realm.

Chapter 28: The First Gate of the Six Supernormal Powers (Ṣaḍabhijñā). 1. The supernormal power of the divine eye (divyacakṣus-abhijñā). 2. The supernormal power of the divine ear (divyaśrotra-abhijñā). 3. The supernormal power of knowing the minds of others (paracitta-jñāna-abhijñā). 4. The supernormal power of recollecting past lives (pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-abhijñā). 5. The supernormal power of bodily mastery (ṛddhi-viṣaya-abhijñā). 6. The supernormal power of the exhaustion of outflows (āsravakṣaya-abhijñā). Regarding the explanation of the six supernormal powers following the discussion of transformations: [it is as follows].
There are three different points of view here.
If one relies on supernormal powers obtained through karmic retribution,
one must first attain those supernormal powers before being able to perform transformations.
If one is to cultivate and attain supernormal powers (abhijñā),
one must first practice the transformations (nirmāṇa) before the supernormal powers can be attained.
Since this section now concerns the sequence of attainment through cultivation,
the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) are explained immediately following the transformation bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*).
These are all termed "powers" (*tong*).
The *Sūtra of the Necklaces* states:
"The spirit is named the Heavenly Mind;
its penetration is named the Nature of Wisdom."
Innate wisdom penetrates and illuminates all without obstruction; therefore,
it is called supernormal power (abhijñā).
First, the supernormal power of the divine eye (*divyacakṣus-abhijñā*): One who cultivates the divine eye,
while within a profound state of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*),
brings forth the abiding of the pure derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*) composed of the four great elements of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
Within the faculty of the eye, one is able to see sentient beings of the six realms of existence as they die here and are born there,
as well as all the various forms and colors of the world;
this is the supernormal power of the divine eye (*divyacakṣurabhijñā*).
Second, the supernormal power of the divine ear (*divya-śrotra-abhijñā*). One who cultivates the divine ear,
while in deep meditative concentration (*dhyāna*),
brings forth and attains a state of pure derivative matter (*upādāya-rūpa*) composed of the four great elements of the form realm (*rūpa-dhātu*).
Within the faculty of hearing, one is able to hear the languages of sentient beings in the six realms of existence as well as the various sounds of the world;
this is the supernormal power of the divine ear (divya-śrotra-abhijñā).
Third is the supernormal power of knowing the minds of others. One who cultivates the knowledge of others' minds,
if within deep meditative concentration,
gives rise to the knowledge of others' minds.
One is then able to know the minds of sentient beings in the six realms of existence as well as their mental factors,
and various objects of focus and thoughts;
this is the supernormal power of knowing the minds of others.
Fourth, the supernormal power of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna*).
One who cultivates the supernormal power of recollecting past lives gives rise to the wisdom of recollecting past lives while within deep meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
He is immediately able to know his own past lives— one life, two lives, hundreds of thousands of millions of lives, even up to eighty thousand great kalpas—
as well as the deeds he performed therein;
he is also able to know the past lives of all sentient beings within the six realms of existence.
And the deeds performed therein—this is the knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsajñāna*).
Fifth is the supernormal power of mastery over the body (*kāyavaiśāradya*). Regarding the cultivation of the supernormal power of the body:
If one attains the supernormal power of the body (*ṛddhi-vidhi-jñāna*) within deep meditative concentration (*dhyāna*),
there are two types of such powers:
first, flying swiftly to reach mountains and obstacles without hindrance.
Second, they are able to transform their own bodies,
the bodies of others, and all things in the world,
exercising mastery according to their will.
This is the supernormal power of mastery over the body.
Sixth, the supernormal power of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya-abhijñā*). Regarding the cultivation of the supernormal power of the exhaustion of outflows:
if, within profound meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), [one perceives...]

When one gives rise to the true wisdom that perceives and contemplates [the nature of reality], the three outflows (*āsrava*) are forever exhausted; this is the supernormal power of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya-abhijñā*). 29. The First Gate of the Nine Successive Attainments (*navānupūrvavihārasamāpatti*).

1. The first dhyāna. 2. The second dhyāna. 3. The third dhyāna. 4. The fourth dhyāna. 5. The sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*). 6. The sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*). 7. The sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*). 8. The sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*). 9. The successive attainment of the cessation of feeling and perception (*saṃjñāvedayitanirodhasamāpatti*). Regarding the explanation of the nine successive attainments following the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*): [The text proceeds as follows:]... [The first dhyāna]... [The second dhyāna]... [The third dhyāna]... [The fourth dhyāna]... [The sphere of infinite space]... [The sphere of infinite consciousness]... [The sphere of nothingness]... [The sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception]... [The successive attainment of the cessation of feeling and perception]. The nine successive attainments are distinguished after the six supernormal powers.
The dhyāna explained above,
although complete in both essence and function,
is entirely contemplative dhyāna (vipaśyanā-dhyāna).
Not yet clearly understanding the characteristics of refined flexibility,
one now wishes to cultivate and practice the essence and function of contemplative meditation (*vipaśyanā*),
so as to bring it to full maturity and enter its essential nature.
Furthermore, because at the time of arising there is no interval in the mind,
it is explained next. Generally speaking,
this refers to the "successive concentrations" (anupūrva-samāpatti).
When entering meditative absorption,
with a profound mind and sharp, keen wisdom,
one is able to enter from one dhyāna into another.
The mind and mind continue in succession without any intervening divergent thoughts;
because they are not mixed, it is called "successive concentration" (anupūrvavihārasamādhi).
The sequential attainment of the first dhyāna: free from all desires and unwholesome states,
with directed thought and sustained evaluation,
and the joy and happiness born of seclusion.
When entering the first dhyāna concentration,
within that first dhyāna concentration, one observes with equanimity and recognizes one's own mind.
With the mind entering in successive stages without a single moment of distracted thought,
one enters the first dhyāna concentration;
this is called the sequential concentration of the first dhyāna.
Regarding the sequential meditative absorption of the second dhyāna:
when entering the second dhyāna from the first dhyāna,
the concentration and insight within this second dhyāna are perfectly balanced.
He recognizes his own mind,
and as that mind enters sequentially,
there is not a single moment of distracted thought intervening before he enters the second dhyāna-concentration.
This is the sequential attainment of the second dhyāna.
Regarding the sequential attainment of the third dhyāna, the mental factors are as clarified in the first and second dhyānas.
Regarding the sequential attainment of the fourth dhyāna, the mental factors are likewise as clarified in the first and second dhyānas.
The successive meditative attainments (*anupūrvavihārasamāpatti*) of the five spheres of infinite space are to be understood in the same manner as those explained for the first and second dhyānas.
The successive meditative attainments of the six spheres of consciousness are likewise to be understood in the same manner as those explained for the first and second dhyānas.
The sequential meditative absorption of the seventh station of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) is also to be understood by analogy with what was explained regarding the first and second dhyānas.

The sequential meditative absorption of the eighth station of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) is also to be understood by analogy with what was explained regarding the first and second dhyānas.

The ninth is the attainment of the successive cessation of perception and feeling (*saṃjñā-vedayita-nirodha-samāpatti*). When one enters the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling from the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,
prior to this attainment:
Recognizing the essential nature of his own mind and vowing to benefit others,
he enters stage by stage, moment by moment,
without any intervening distracted thoughts, until he enters the meditative attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling (*nirodha-samāpatti*).

The essence of the nine successive attainments is precisely the three samādhis;
there is only a difference in the names and numbers resulting from their separation or combination.
There are slight differences in their respective systems of establishment;
such is the meaning of these various points. Why is this so?
The nine successive concentrations (navānupūrvavihārasamāpatti) universally encompass all dhyānas;
they possess no separate essence of their own.
The three samādhis are likewise so.
Thus we know that their essence is not different from other dharmas,
yet they have no fixed name.
Although the names and numbers of the nine concentrations are many,
the intermediate ones are not taken;
although the names and numbers of the samādhis are few, [they are nonetheless included].
Yet, including the intermediate [dhyāna], these together comprise the nine concentrations (*samādhi*).
Generally, they are designated as "samādhis" based on the principles and phenomena of the various dhyānas;
generally, they receive their names based on the phenomena and principles of the various dhyānas.
This constitutes a slight distinction;
therefore, following the nine meditative absorptions (dhyāna), the three samādhis are explained.
Regarding "samādhi" in its general sense:
Samādhi— translated in the Qin language as "the sphere of right mental activity"—
is this mind that has existed from time immemorial.
It is always bent and not upright;
because it attains this straightness,
it is called samādhi.

First, the samādhi with both vitarka and vicāra: if one enters various meditative absorptions with a mind associated with emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, this occurs within the first dhyāna and its preparatory stages (prayoga).
Thus, all dhyānas accompanied by vitarka and vicāra are entirely upright; therefore,
they are called the samādhi with vitarka and vicāra.
Second, the samādhi with no vitarka and with vicāra: if one enters various meditative absorptions with a mind associated with emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness,
and contemplates the intermediate dhyāna,
then all such dhyānas are characterized by no vitarka and with vicāra.
Because they are all entirely upright, it is called the samādhi with no vitarka and with vicāra.
Third is the samādhi with neither vitarka nor vicāra: if one enters various meditative absorptions with a mind associated with emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
In the contemplation of the meditative absorption without directed thought and without sustained thought,
one contemplates all concentrations from the second dhyāna up to the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling as being without directed thought and without sustained thought.
Because they are all entirely upright, it is called the samādhi without applied thought and without sustained thought (*avitarko 'vicāraḥ samādhiḥ*). Chapter 31:

The First Gate of the Lion’s Unfurled Vigor Samādhi (*siṃhavijṛmbhita-samādhi*). There are two kinds of lion’s unfurled vigor samādhi: first, unfurled entry; second, unfurled exit. Regarding the lion’s unfurled vigor samādhi, it is explained following the three preceding samādhis.
In the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, the Buddha himself spoke with sincerity:
"The bodhisattva, relying on the nine successive concentrations,
enters the Lion’s Bound-Forth Samādhi."
Since the characteristics of the three samādhis and the nine meditative absorptions (dhyāna) are identical,
they are explained immediately following the three samādhis; thus,
there is no contradiction in their meaning.
That which is called "the lion’s bound" is a metaphor used to manifest the Dharma;
it is like the lion’s bound in the world.
For two reasons: first, to shake off dust and dirt;
second, to be able to run forward and backward with a swiftness that surpasses all other beasts.
This samādhi is likewise:
first, it vigorously eliminates the subtle and unconscious delusions that obstruct meditative concentration;
second, it enables swift and uninterrupted entry into and emergence from it.
It is distinct from the various dhyānas and samādhis previously attained;
therefore, it is named the Lion’s Bound-Forth Samādhi (*siṃhavijṛmbhita-samādhi*).
First, entering dhyāna with vigor: as for the Lion’s Bound-Forth entry into samādhi—
Detached from sensual desires and unwholesome states,
with directed thought and sustained evaluation, he enters the first dhyāna;
in this manner, he successively enters the second, third, and fourth dhyānas.
The sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness,
the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,
and the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling.
This is the "vigorous entry.
Second is the vigorous emergence from meditative concentration (*dhyāna-vikrīḍita*). Regarding the "lion’s vigorous emergence":
one arises from the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling (*nirodhasamāpatti*).
He returns to enter the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;
from the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception he arises and returns to enter the sphere of nothingness.
In this way, from the sphere of consciousness, the sphere of infinite space, the fourth, third, second, and first dhyānas,
down to emerging into the distracted mind—
this is called "emergence through mastery."

32. The First Gate of the Samādhi of Transcendence (Samatikrama-samādhi). Chapter Thirty-two: The First Gate of the Samādhi of Transcendence. 1. Single-leap entry. 2. Single-leap exit. Next, regarding the "Lion’s Sport" (Siṃhavikrīḍita) that explains transcendence:
In the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, the Buddha himself spoke with sincere words:
"A bodhisattva, relying on the *siṃhavikrīḍita-samādhi*,
enters the *vyutkrāntaka-samādhi*."
The reason they are called "transcendent" is that they are able to surpass all stages,
entering and emerging from them with mastery.
Therefore, it is called "transcending. What is meant by "transcending into samādhi"?
It is to be free from all desires and from unwholesome, evil states.
With directed thought and sustained thought, and with the joy and happiness born of seclusion, he enters the first dhyāna.

Arising from the first dhyāna, he transcends to enter the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. Arising from the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, he enters the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling.
Emerging from the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling, he re-enters the first dhyāna;
emerging from the first dhyāna, he enters the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling;
emerging from the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling, he enters the second dhyāna.
Emerging from the second dhyāna, he enters the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling;
emerging from the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling, he enters the third dhyāna;
emerging from the third dhyāna, he enters the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling.
Emerging from the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling, he enters the fourth dhyāna;
emerging from the fourth dhyāna, he enters the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling;
emerging from the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling, he enters the sphere of infinite space.
Arising from the sphere of infinite space, he enters the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling;
arising from the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling, he enters the sphere of infinite consciousness;
arising from the sphere of infinite consciousness, he enters the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling.
Emerging from the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling, one enters the sphere of nothingness;
emerging from the sphere of nothingness, one enters the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling;
emerging from the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling, one enters the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Arising from the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, one enters the meditative attainment of the cessation of feeling and perception;
this is the characteristic of the samādhis entered by all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
If a śrāvaka can enter only one such state, he is able to transcend it.
Yet they cannot transcend these two;
how much less can they transcend them with the mastery explained above?
Within this, it is clarified that there are three ways of transcending and entering.
First, sequential entry with skipping;
second, reverse entry with skipping;
third, both sequential and reverse entry with skipping.
The detailed meaning of "subtle mind" can be understood by oneself.
Second, the samādhi of transcendence: what is called the samādhi of transcendence?
It is when one emerges from the cessation of perception and feeling and enters into a state of distracted consciousness.
Arising from the state of distracted mind, he enters the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling;
arising from the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling, he returns to abide in the state of distracted mind;
arising from the state of distracted mind, he enters the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
From the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, one arises and dwells in a distracted state of mind;
from that distracted state of mind, one arises and enters the sphere of nothingness;
from the sphere of nothingness, one arises and dwells in a distracted state of mind.
From the state of distracted mind, one arises and enters the sphere of infinite consciousness;
from the sphere of infinite consciousness, one arises and dwells in the state of distracted mind;
from the state of distracted mind, one arises and enters the sphere of infinite space.
From the sphere of infinite space, one arises and dwells in a distracted state of mind;
from the distracted state of mind, one arises and enters the fourth dhyāna;
from the fourth dhyāna, one arises and dwells in a distracted state of mind.
Arising from the state of distracted mind, one enters the third dhyāna;
arising from the third dhyāna, one abides in the state of distracted mind.
Arising from the state of distracted mind, one enters the second dhyāna.
From the second dhyāna, one arises and dwells in the distracted mind;
from the distracted mind, one arises and enters the first dhyāna;
from the first dhyāna, one arises and dwells in the distracted mind.
This is the characteristic of the samādhis that transcend [the world] of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
If a Śrāvaka were to transcend,
they could only transcend and emerge from a single dhyāna.
Yet they cannot transcend these two;
how much less can they transcend them with mastery?
Within this, there are three kinds of transcendence.
First, ascending transcendence;
second, descending transcendence;
third, both ascending and descending transcendence.
The three types of successive entry at the beginning and the three types at the end combine to form six types of transcendent samādhi.
Regarding these six samādhis, the Tathāgata—
And thus enter into *nirvāṇa*.
This concludes the section on the common meditative practices (*dhyāna*) of the three vehicles (*triyāna*).
